judgement.human_basis: The highest evidence level is a phase 2 single-arm trial of guadecitabine (azacitidine analog) plus atezolizumab in metastatic urothelial carcinoma, which showed no RECIST responses and closed for futility (PMID 36928921).
judgement.caveats: Human evidence uses guadecitabine, a related hypomethylating prodrug, combined with immunotherapy rather than azacitidine alone; no azacitidine monotherapy phase 2/3 human urothelial carcinoma data were available, and only phase 1 combination trials with cisplatin/gemcitabine (PMID 29615077, 33472913) exist otherwise, which report tolerability rather than efficacy.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Single-arm phase I trial in 13 dogs with invasive TCC treated with intravesical MMC showed 5/13 (38%) partial remission, above the 20% ORR threshold for single-arm cancer studies, plus 7/13 stable disease.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase 3 trials and an IPD meta-analysis show MMC reduces recurrence/improves locoregional control versus TURBT alone or radiotherapy alone (BC2001, meta-analysis, ATLAS, ENVISION), while other phase 3 trials found no significant benefit from adding or intensifying MMC (HIVEC-1 hyperthermia vs normothermia; ANZUP BCG+MMC vs BCG alone).
judgement.caveats: US labels only cover gastric/pancreatic adenocarcinoma, not bladder cancer, so no approval-level evidence applies; veterinary evidence is a small single-arm dose-escalation study without a comparator arm, limiting direct comparability to controlled human trials.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A multimodal single-arm trial combining prednisone with toceranib and radiation therapy achieved a 76.4% objective response rate in dogs with unresectable MCT, exceeding the 20% threshold. A separate pilot study only examined histological/proliferation markers after short-course prednisone and did not assess clinical response, so it is indeterminate rather than contradictory.
judgement.human_basis: The only retrieved human-relevant record is actually a canine (veterinary) phase-1 study of a different drug (KPT-335) that used low-dose prednisone merely for toxicity management, not as a treatment for human mastocytoma. No human trials or approvals for prednisone in human mastocytoma were found.
judgement.caveats: No genuine human clinical evidence for mastocytoma (a rare human mast cell neoplasm) was available; the single retrieved 'human' record is actually a canine study, so the human side lacks any disease-specific efficacy data for comparison.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The only veterinary RCT (PMID:21529238) compared three injectable opioid-adjunct combinations (butorphanol, hydromorphone, buprenorphine) for canine castration without a placebo or no-treatment control; all combinations produced acceptable anesthesia, with DKH needing supplemental isoflurane most often. This is a comparative/dose-finding study, not a placebo-controlled superiority or single-arm outcome trial, so it is indeterminate.
judgement.human_basis: Hydromorphone is FDA-approved (multiple ANDAs/NDA) for management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic, which covers postoperative pain, representing the highest level of evidence (US approval).
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single small comparative RCT without a placebo/no-treatment arm, precluding a definitive positive/negative call; human evidence rests on broad opioid labeling rather than a disease-specific pivotal trial for postoperative pain.

judgement.veterinary_basis: All vet RCTs used morphine as a comparator or combination partner against other active drugs, not placebo; none show a controlled failure or clear single-arm response threshold. Studies focused on dose-finding, motor/respiratory tolerability, or comparisons among opioid combinations, not on morphine's efficacy versus no treatment.

judgement.human_basis: The pivotal placebo-controlled PARAMEDIC-2 RCT (n=8014) found epinephrine significantly improved the primary outcome of 30-day survival versus placebo (3.2% vs 2.4%, OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.06-1.82, P=.02), though neurologic outcome was not significantly different (PMID:30021076).
judgement.caveats: Veterinary positivity rests on a secondary survival endpoint (1-hour survival) rather than the primary ROSC endpoint, which showed no difference; human positivity is based on the primary survival endpoint of PARAMEDIC-2, but favorable neurologic outcome was not improved and no US label covers cardiac arrest specifically.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The single RCT (PMID:22092625) compared vasopressin to active comparator epinephrine, not placebo/no-treatment; ROSC rates were similar (P=.20) though epinephrine showed better 1-hour survival, so this does not meet the strict criteria for a 'negative' controlled trial against placebo.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase-3 RCTs and meta-analyses show conflicting results: some trials (PMID 19139319, 14711909-asystole subgroup) found vasopressin combinations improved ROSC/survival vs placebo/epinephrine, while others (PMID 18596271, 11463411, 36476543, 35490936) and meta-analyses (PMID 35934565, 30980877) found no survival benefit over epinephrine or placebo. No US approval exists for cardiac arrest; labels (L0-L5) cover vasodilatory shock only.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to one head-to-head trial against an active comparator (epinephrine) rather than placebo, limiting classification to indeterminate. Human evidence spans many phase-3 RCTs and meta-analyses with genuinely conflicting results depending on arrest setting (in-hospital vs out-of-hospital), rhythm subtype (asystole vs VF), and co-administered agents (steroids), supporting a mixed classification rather than a clear positive or negative signal.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Only a single small, uncontrolled dose-finding trial (11 dogs) assessed metronomic cyclophosphamide in canine STS, measuring Treg numbers and tumor microvessel density rather than tumor response; no controlled efficacy endpoint was reported (PMID:21736624).
judgement.human_basis: Phase 3/meta-analysis level evidence is mixed: SWOG phase 3 (PMID 3295129) showed no survival/response benefit from adding cyclophosphamide, EORTC adjuvant CYVADIC (PMID 8201375) improved relapse-free survival but not overall survival, and the RMS2005 phase 3 trial's primary endpoint (DFS) narrowly missed significance at initial report (PMID 31562043) though later reached significance with mature follow-up (PMID 40053891); a meta-analysis (PMID 33501892) showed a significant OS/RFS benefit for cyclophosphamide-containing regimens.
judgement.caveats: US labels do not list soft tissue sarcoma as an approved indication for cyclophosphamide, so approval-level evidence is absent; human evidence largely derives from pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma trials using cyclophosphamide as part of combination regimens rather than as monotherapy, limiting direct comparability to the single-agent canine metronomic study.

judgement.veterinary_basis: An RCT in dogs undergoing MRI for neurological diagnosis found propofol induction resulted in significantly better recovery scores than alfaxalone (SDS p=0.014, VAS p=0.017), demonstrating superiority to an active comparator (PMID 22117934).
judgement.human_basis: Propofol is FDA-approved (multiple ANDAs and Diprivan NDA) for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia, which is the standard approach for sedation/anesthesia required for neurological diagnostic imaging procedures such as MRI.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single comparator RCT versus alfaxalone rather than placebo, but it meets the superiority-to-comparator criterion; human approval is a general anesthesia indication not specific to neurological diagnostics but covers the intent of anesthesia for diagnostic procedures.

judgement.human_basis: US labels approve carvedilol for chronic heart failure, post-MI LV dysfunction, and hypertension, but none specifically address chronic valvular heart disease as a disease-modifying indication; no human trials for this specific condition were retrieved.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to an uncontrolled retrospective series in preclinical-stage dogs, and human evidence is indirect (general HF/hypertension labeling) rather than specific to valvular heart disease, so no direct comparison of disease-modifying efficacy in CVHD can be made for either species.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Single-arm trial in 28 dogs with bladder TCC showed partial remission in 36% and stable disease in 50%, exceeding the 20% ORR threshold for single-arm efficacy.
judgement.human_basis: Phase 3 trials of vinblastine-containing regimens (CMV, MVAC) versus cystectomy alone or no chemotherapy showed significant survival benefit in muscle-invasive/locally advanced urothelial carcinoma (e.g., 10-year survival 30%->36% with CMV; median survival 46->77 months with neoadjuvant MVAC). Comparative phase 3 trials (GC vs MVAC, ddMVAC vs GC) confirmed MVAC-based regimens as an effective standard, though some secondary comparisons (VESPER 5-year OS) did not show superiority over another active regimen.
judgement.caveats: Vinblastine in humans is almost always used as part of combination regimens (MVAC/CMV) rather than as monotherapy, unlike the canine single-agent trial; human phase 3 evidence largely derives from comparisons against another active chemotherapy regimen rather than placebo, though early trials versus surgery/no-chemo controls were positive.

This meets the primary efficacy endpoint criterion for a positive classification.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple fluoxetine drug labels (L0-L5) explicitly list Obsessive Compulsive Disorder as an approved indication, representing the highest level of evidence (US approval). judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is from a single small RCT (25 dogs) with delayed onset of significance versus placebo; human evidence is robust with FDA-approved indication and multiple positive pivotal RCTs, though some individual trials show mixed or non-significant findings for adjunct therapies.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The pivotal randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial (PMID:22295869, n=34) found adjunctive levetiracetam did not significantly reduce seizure frequency versus placebo (P=.310), meeting the criteria for a negative controlled trial. A second controlled study (PMID:26639829) also found LEV monotherapy ineffective versus phenobarbital, though as an active comparator trial it does not independently qualify as negative under the strict criteria.
judgement.human_basis: Levetiracetam holds FDA approval as monotherapy/adjunctive therapy for partial-onset seizures, myoclonic seizures in JME, and primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures across multiple age groups (L1-L5), representing disease-modifying seizure control indications. This approval constitutes the highest level of evidence and is positive.
judgement.caveats: The vet-approved label evidence reflects broad efficacy across seizure types and ages, while the single placebo-controlled canine RCT was underpowered (22/34 completers) and showed a numerically favorable but non-significant trend, so the negative classification rests on a single moderately-sized trial; human evidence includes many head-to-head trials (e.g., SANAD II) showing LEV is not superior to comparators like lamotrigine/valproate, though it remains an approved, effective antiseizure drug overall.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, blinded, controlled trial in 184 cats (PMID:22309012) showed dexmedetomidine premedication significantly improved intubation success, reduced induction and maintenance drug requirements, and improved postoperative analgesia compared with placebo, meeting primary efficacy endpoints. The dog study (PMID:31197847) was a pharmacokinetic/bioavailability study only, providing no efficacy endpoint (indeterminate).
judgement.human_basis: Dexmedetomidine is FDA-approved (multiple ANDAs and NDA021038) for ICU and procedural sedation in adults and pediatric patients, representing the highest level of evidence. Supporting phase 3 trials (e.g., PMID:22436955) demonstrated non-inferiority to standard sedatives and improved secondary outcomes, consistent with approval.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single positive cat RCT and an indeterminate dog PK study, so species generalization is incomplete. Human evidence, while anchored by approval, includes some later large RCTs (e.g., PMID:31112380, PMID:33528922, PMID:40388916) showing no superiority over comparators for certain hard outcomes (mortality, extubation time), though these do not negate the approved sedation indication.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, double-blinded crossover trial in 7 dogs with CHF from mitral valve disease found torsemide equivalent to furosemide in controlling clinical signs, with likely greater diuresis (PMID:22364690).
judgement.human_basis: Torsemide is FDA-approved for treatment of edema associated with heart failure (L0-L5), a broad indication that includes heart failure due to valvular disease; multiple phase-3/meta-analyses further support efficacy on functional status and hospitalization outcomes, though mortality benefit is not consistently shown.
judgement.caveats: The veterinary evidence is a small (n=7) non-inferiority crossover pilot rather than a large superiority trial; the human approval is for heart failure edema generally, not specifically mitral valve disease, and human RCT/meta-analysis evidence is mixed regarding mortality benefit despite consistent improvement in hospitalization and functional class.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial in 19 dogs with status epilepticus/ARS found IV levetiracetam produced a 56% responder rate versus 10% for placebo, with dogs on placebo requiring significantly more diazepam boluses (PMID:22295898).
judgement.human_basis: The pivotal ESETT phase 3 trial (design paper PMID:24001084, results PMID:31774955, age-stratified analysis PMID:32203691) showed IV levetiracetam achieved seizure cessation and improved consciousness in ~47% of benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus patients, performing comparably to fosphenytoin and valproate with no signal of inferiority or failure.
judgement.caveats: The canine trial's p-value for the primary endpoint was 0.06 (borderline), and the pivotal human ESETT trial was an active-comparator (no placebo arm) design, so 'positive' reflects comparable efficacy to accepted standard-of-care drugs rather than formal superiority or non-inferiority margin testing; no US label specifically lists status epilepticus as an indication.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple US amoxicillin labels (L0-L4) include an approved indication for skin and skin structure infections caused by susceptible Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and E. coli, representing the highest evidence tier.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, double-blinded trial (PMID 22681547) found oral methylprednisolone induced remission of pruritus (score ≤2/10) in allergic cats at a mean dose of 1.41 mg/kg, with efficacy comparable to triamcinolone. Both drugs met the pre-defined remission endpoint, satisfying the positive criterion for an RCT meeting its primary efficacy endpoint.
judgement.human_basis: US labels (L2, L3, L4) list methylprednisolone sodium succinate as indicated for control of severe allergic conditions including atopic dermatitis and drug hypersensitivity reactions, which encompass allergic pruritus. Supporting phase-level evidence (e.g., PMID 18284403, 17298428) also shows methylprednisolone aceponate reduces pruritus/itch in atopic dermatitis trials.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single active-comparator (non-placebo) RCT without a placebo arm, and human approval covers allergic dermatologic conditions broadly rather than 'pruritus' as a standalone indication; species differ (cat vs human) and formulations (oral vs topical/IM) vary across records.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple RCTs show TMP-SMX superior to placebo for skin abscess cure (83.1% vs 68.9%, PMID:28657870), reduces failure/recurrence in MRSA abscess after drainage (PMID:26578074), and trimethoprim-polymyxin B cream outperformed fusidic acid for pyoderma (PMID:3030946). No US label specifically covers skin infection as an indication.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was rated 'fair' rather than 'good' and derived from a systematic review rather than a single pivotal trial; human evidence spans several distinct skin infection subtypes (abscess, pyoderma) rather than a single well-defined condition, and a large stepped-wedge community trial for impetigo control showed no significant effect but was excluded as it tested a multi-component program rather than trimethoprim monotherapy efficacy.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A masked RCT in 31 dogs with spontaneous CKD found ~50% lower mortality from uremic crises with a chitosan/phosphate-binder/alkalinizer supplement vs placebo (P=0.015), meeting its primary endpoint.
judgement.human_basis: Phase 3 RCTs and meta-analyses on binders assessing disease-modifying outcomes (mortality/cardiovascular events) in CKD are inconsistent: some show benefit (sevelamer reduced all-cause mortality vs calcium-based binders in PMID 22241819 and in meta-analysis PMID 40576086), while others found no significant difference (lanthanum vs calcium carbonate on CV events, PMID 34003226; cinacalcet vs placebo on death/CV events, PMID 23121374; network meta-analysis showing no mortality benefit vs placebo, PMID 27461851).
judgement.caveats: Veterinary trial used a combination supplement (chitosan+phosphate binders+alkalinizers), not a single binder class, limiting direct molecule-level comparability; human evidence for disease-modifying (mortality/CV) outcomes with binders is heterogeneous across binder types and comparators, whereas most FDA-relevant human evidence targets symptomatic control of hyperphosphatemia/hyperkalemia rather than CKD disease modification.

judgement.human_basis: In phase 2 RCTs (PMID 31629805, 41037525) topical triamcinolone 0.1% achieved substantial EASI and IGA improvements versus vehicle/baseline (e.g., 47.1% EASI75, 25.5% IGA success), confirming efficacy for atopic dermatitis even though a JAK inhibitor performed somewhat better.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single active-comparator RCT without a placebo arm, and human phase-2 evidence for triamcinolone comes mainly as an active comparator in trials designed to test a competing drug rather than as a primary efficacy trial of triamcinolone itself; no US label indication exists for either species for allergic dermatitis specifically.

judgement.human_basis: Morphine sulfate products carry US FDA approval for management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic, which covers symptomatic pain relief in patients with disc herniation as reflected in its routine use as background/rescue analgesic in multiple human perioperative IVD herniation trials.
judgement.caveats: The human evidence rests on a general opioid pain label rather than a disease-specific pivotal trial for disc herniation; multiple RCTs used morphine only as a rescue/comparator analgesic rather than testing morphine itself as the primary intervention, so direct efficacy comparisons are indirect.

judgement.human_basis: Large RCTs and meta-analyses on gabapentin for postoperative pain show inconsistent results: some meta-analyses and RCTs (e.g., 36404458, 32654111, 38935013, 28551445) show reduced pain/opioid use, while others (e.g., 40663783 GAP trial, 32235144 spine surgery, 28741425 tonsillectomy, 34637958 sciatica meta-analysis) show no benefit or worse outcomes. No US label indication exists for postoperative pain, so phase-3/meta-analysis is the highest evidence tier, and it is mixed.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single RCT with a small trend toward benefit that did not reach significance, so classification as negative follows the strict rule but borderline results exist. Human evidence is highly heterogeneous across surgical contexts, doses, and comparators, making the overall human classification mixed rather than clearly positive or negative; no FDA-approved indication for postoperative pain exists.

judgement.caveats: No US label covers systemic illness/SIRS/sepsis for acetylcysteine, and additional smaller RCTs (bipolar comorbidity, ICU phagocytosis) showed only tangential or mixed physiological effects not reflecting disease-modifying benefit.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (PMID:32707333) failed its primary endpoint of improving QOL/activity in cats with subclinical HCM, and a companion observational cohort (PMID:23684504) showed no survival benefit.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase-3 RCTs (LIFE, SILVHIA) and a meta-analysis show atenolol produces less regression of left ventricular hypertrophy and less cardiovascular/stroke benefit than comparator agents (losartan, irbesartan), and one RCT showed LV mass actually increased with atenolol versus isradipine. No US label indication exists for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; atenolol is only approved for hypertension.
judgement.caveats: Vet evidence is limited to feline subclinical HCM with small samples and one non-randomized cohort; human evidence pertains to hypertension-induced LV hypertrophy rather than primary/genetic HCM, and reflects comparative inferiority to other antihypertensives rather than placebo-controlled failure, limiting direct translational comparability.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The only veterinary study (PMID:23758137) was a nonblinded, uncontrolled observational trial in 12 CHF dogs showing only tolerability and lipid/inflammatory marker changes, not validated outcome improvement (echo, QOL) required for a positive call.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple RCTs in human heart failure/CHD populations show inconsistent results: some (GREACE, MIRACL-related, small endothelial-function RCT) report benefit, while HF-ACTION and ALPS-AMI RCTs failed to show benefit on their primary endpoints; no RCT specifically targets CHF due to mitral valve disease.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single small uncontrolled pilot study lacking validated outcome endpoints; human evidence, while more extensive, addresses heterogeneous heart-failure etiologies (mostly ischemic) rather than mitral valve disease specifically, and shows mixed RCT results, precluding a clear concordant/discordant call.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized cat trial (PMID:23157371) showed vinblastine achieved comparable response rates, PFS and survival to vincristine within a COP protocol, indicating efficacy. A dog phase II dose-finding trial (PMID:30117260) found only 1/14 (7%) partial response at 2 mg/m2 (below the 20% threshold, single-arm/dose-escalation), yielding indeterminate results at the tested dose.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase 3 randomized trials of vinblastine-containing regimens (ABVD, AVD, A+AVD, N-AVD) met their efficacy endpoints, including ECHELON-1 (5-year PFS 82.2% vs 75.3%, HR 0.68) and S1826 (3-year PFS 93% vs 82%, HR 0.37) in Hodgkin lymphoma. No US label exists specifically for vinblastine in lymphoma, so phase 3 evidence is the highest level, and all such trials are positive.
judgement.caveats: Vinblastine is almost always used as part of multi-agent combination regimens (COP, ABVD, AVD) in both species, making attribution of efficacy to vinblastine alone difficult; the canine data suggest single-agent vinblastine has limited activity at low doses, while human data reflect combination regimens with vinblastine as one component of a highly effective multi-drug protocol.

judgement.human_basis: A 2026 network meta-analysis of 47 RCTs found antihistamines (including cetirizine) produced statistically significant but clinically negligible reductions in AD severity and itch, well below minimal important differences; individual RCTs are inconsistent, with some showing significant benefit on pruritus/symptoms (PMID:8067594, 8430920, 11204513, 22313287) and others (ETAC trials) showing similar SCORAD improvement in both cetirizine and placebo groups with no disease-modifying effect on the atopic march overall.
judgement.caveats: No US label covers atopic dermatitis for cetirizine (labels are for urticaria, allergic rhinitis, or ocular itching only), so human evidence rests on RCT/meta-analysis level; the veterinary negative finding is from a single, albeit well-designed, RCT while human evidence is heterogeneous across many RCTs of varying quality and endpoints, limiting direct comparability.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Two RCTs in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease showed benefit: the 2013 study found lower cardiac/renal death rates with spironolactone added to conventional therapy, and the 2021 BESST trial showed spironolactone+benazepril was superior to benazepril alone on the primary composite endpoint (OR 0.56, P=.04).
judgement.human_basis: Spironolactone is FDA-approved for NYHA Class III-IV heart failure with reduced ejection fraction to increase survival and reduce hospitalization, based on positive pivotal evidence (e.g., RALES showing 30% mortality reduction).
judgement.caveats: Human approval and most supporting trials (RALES, EMPHASIS) address heart failure broadly by ejection fraction phenotype rather than valvular etiology specifically, and later trials in HFpEF (TOPCAT) and other settings were negative or mixed, though these do not override the top-level approval evidence per the instructed hierarchy.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Single-dose, active-controlled (not placebo-controlled) RCT in 28 cats showed a statistically significant but clinically negligible reduction in LVOT peak velocity with ivabradine (0.32 m/s vs 2.53 m/s for atenolol, P<.0001), an acute pharmacodynamic study not assessing disease-modifying outcomes.
judgement.human_basis: No human trials or FDA-approved indications for ivabradine in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with LVOT obstruction were identified; all US labels list only heart failure with reduced ejection fraction indications.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single acute-dose, active-controlled (non-placebo) trial with negligible clinical effect, and no human efficacy data for HCM/LVOTO exist, making direct comparison unreliable.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Two large randomized, placebo-controlled trials of the JAK1 inhibitor oclacitinib (class-analogue) in dogs with allergic/atopic dermatitis (n=436 and n=299) met primary pruritus/dermatitis endpoints with high significance (P<0.0001) versus placebo.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase 3 RCTs of abrocitinib and upadacitinib (class-analogues) met coprimary IGA/EASI-75 endpoints versus placebo and were superior to dupilumab in head-to-head trials; network meta-analyses confirm high-certainty efficacy for these JAK inhibitors in atopic dermatitis. No AD indication is present on the tofacitinib labels provided, so approval-level evidence is absent for this specific drug list.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is for oclacitinib, a class-analogue JAK1 inhibitor, not the exact human drugs; human top-level evidence rests on phase 3 RCTs/meta-analyses of abrocitinib and upadacitinib (also class-analogues to each other) rather than a formal US label indication for atopic dermatitis in the provided label set, which only covers tofacitinib for RA/PsA/AS/UC/pcJIA.

L0.indications: INDICATIONS AND USAGE Hypertension Enalapril maleate is indicated for the treatment of hypertension. Enalapril maleate is effective alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents, especially thiazide-type diuretics. The blood pressure lowering effects of enalapril maleate and thiazides are approximately additive. Heart Failure Enalapril maleate is indicated for the treatment of symptomatic congestive heart failure, usually in combination with diuretics and digitalis. In these patients enalapril maleate improves symptoms, increases survival, and decreases the frequency of hospitalization (see CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Heart Failure, Mortality Trials for details and limitations of survival trials). Asymptomatic Left Ventricular Dysfunction In clinically stable asymptomatic patients with left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤35 percent), enalapril maleate decreases the rate of development of overt heart failure and decreases the incidence of hospitalization for heart failure (see CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Heart Failure, Mortality Trials for details and limitations of survival trials). In using enalapril maleate consideration should be given to the fact that another angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, captopril, has caused agranulocytosis, particularly in patients with renal impairment or collagen vascular disease, and that available data are insufficient to show that enalapril maleate does not have a similar risk (see WARNINGS, Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis )

judgement.veterinary_basis: Only one small observational case series (PMID:24051253) describes 4 animals with presumptive hypertensive encephalopathy treated with amlodipine ± enalapril; no controlled trial of enalapril for canine/feline hypertension was provided.
judgement.human_basis: Enalapril maleate is FDA-approved for treatment of hypertension (labels L0-L5), and multiple phase 3/RCTs (e.g., PMID 2835964, 2216994, 3001605) confirm significant blood-pressure lowering versus placebo/comparators.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a small uncontrolled case series without a dedicated controlled trial of enalapril monotherapy for hypertension in dogs/cats, precluding a definitive positive/negative classification despite robust human approval data.

judgement.veterinary_basis: In a randomized, double-blind controlled trial (PMID:24112400), budesonide achieved a 78% remission rate in dogs with IBD, statistically indistinguishable from the 69% remission rate with prednisone, demonstrating efficacy comparable to standard therapy in a controlled setting.
judgement.human_basis: Budesonide delayed-release capsules (L2) are FDA-approved for treatment of mild to moderate active Crohn's disease and for maintenance of remission, representing the highest level of evidence (US approval) for an IBD indication.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single controlled trial against an active comparator (prednisone) rather than placebo, so 'positive' reflects comparable efficacy to standard-of-care rather than superiority; human approval is specifically for Crohn's disease (ileal/ascending colon) rather than ulcerative colitis, where phase 3 and meta-analytic evidence is more mixed for topical formulations.

judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a small, non-randomized, non-blinded study assessing a surgical inflammatory biomarker (CRP) rather than pyometra resolution; no human pyometra data exist, so the comparison rests on absence of relevant human evidence and non-disease-modifying veterinary endpoints.

judgement.human_basis: Dexmedetomidine is FDA-approved for ICU sedation of mechanically ventilated adults and for procedural/non-invasive sedation in adults and pediatric patients (labels L0-L5), representing the highest level of evidence.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is drawn mainly from head-to-head comparator trials (not placebo-controlled failures) so true 'negative' classification is avoided per rules, but efficacy relative to comparators varies by study; human evidence is dominated by regulatory approval, while phase 3 trials in critically ill ICU patients show mixed mortality/duration outcomes (e.g., PMID:31112380, PMID:40388916) that are not reflected in the top-level approval evidence.

judgement.human_basis: Direct treatment RCTs in patients with established atopic dermatitis/eczema show benefit: DHA supplementation significantly reduced SCORAD versus control (PMID 18241260), hempseed oil improved clinical symptoms and skin barrier measures (PMID 16019622), and GLA (evening primrose oil) significantly improved overall AD severity in infants (PMID 7924900); most other RCTs concern prevention in pregnancy/infancy rather than treatment of existing disease and show mixed/negative prevention results, but the treatment-focused evidence is consistently positive.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single RCT of a topical combination product (PUFAs plus essential oils), not oral PUFA alone, limiting attribution of effect to PUFAs specifically; human evidence is dominated by prenatal/postnatal allergy-prevention trials (mostly negative or mixed) rather than treatment of diagnosed AD, and the few direct treatment RCTs are small, unblinded in some cases, and not FDA phase-classified, so the 'positive' human classification rests on a small subset of disease-modifying treatment trials rather than a large pivotal trial or approval.

judgement.human_basis: US labels for praziquantel (L0, L1) approve it only for schistosomiasis and liver fluke (trematode) infections, not for nematode or cestode infections; the retrieved human RCTs and observational studies address safety/tolerability of co-administered anthelmintics rather than efficacy against nematode/cestode infection specifically.
judgement.caveats: Human evidence base largely consists of safety/acceptability studies of mass drug administration programs rather than controlled efficacy trials against nematode or cestode infections specifically; praziquantel's approved human indications (schistosomiasis, liver flukes) are trematode infections, not the nematode/cestode indication being compared, limiting direct cross-species comparability.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple US labels (e.g., L0-L5) approve isoflurane for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia without restriction based on intracranial pathology, representing the highest level of evidence. A supporting RCT (PMID 3260082) shows isoflurane reduces cerebral blood flow and oxygen consumption, consistent with its established anesthetic use.
judgement.caveats: The vet trial was a comparator (not placebo) study showing isoflurane inferior to propofol on secondary hemodynamic/recovery measures, not a strict efficacy failure; the human evidence is a broad anesthesia approval not specific to intracranial disease, and the cited human RCT excluded patients with intracranial disease.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The single vet RCT (PMID:24673608) compared short-duration TMP-SMX to long-duration cephalexin (active comparator, not placebo) and found no significant difference in cure rates, with no pre-specified non-inferiority margin; long-term cure was only 50%.
judgement.human_basis: TMP-SMX (co-trimoxazole) carries FDA-approved labeling for urinary tract infections due to susceptible organisms (L1-L4), and multiple phase-level RCTs and meta-analyses confirm efficacy for uncomplicated cystitis (e.g., PMID 34313686, PMID 38587648).
judgement.caveats: The veterinary study used an active comparator rather than placebo, and no explicit non-inferiority margin was pre-specified, making it impossible to classify as positive or negative per the strict criteria; human evidence is robust with a long-standing US-approved indication.

judgement.human_basis: Large RCTs of permethrin-based interventions for cutaneous leishmaniasis show inconsistent results: permethrin-impregnated uniforms failed to significantly reduce CL (PMID 12795775), a multifaceted intervention including permethrin repellent showed a non-significant 58% reduction (PMID 17361851), while permethrin-impregnated bednets/chaddars significantly reduced ACL incidence by ~65% (PMID 11127233).
judgement.caveats: No US label covers leishmaniasis for permethrin; approved indication is scabies only. Human evidence derives from vector-control field trials rather than pharmacologic disease-modifying trials, and veterinary evidence is a mixed-design systematic review combining several agents including permethrin spot-ons.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Ciclosporin is an approved, effective treatment for canine atopic dermatitis; PMID:25496303 confirms comparable efficacy to oclacitinib with non-inferiority met at some time points, and multiple guideline reviews (PMID:26276051, 41303472) list it as a first-line effective systemic therapy.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple placebo-controlled and phase-3 trials (PMID 8204472, 28967549, 37722926, 33074565 meta-analysis) show cyclosporine significantly reduces disease severity versus placebo or is non-inferior/superior to comparators in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; though newer biologics show larger effect sizes, cyclosporine itself meets efficacy endpoints consistently.
judgement.caveats: Neither species has an FDA-labeled indication explicitly naming 'atopic dermatitis' for cyclosporine (veterinary approval is per abstract claim, not label text provided); human evidence relies on older placebo-controlled trials and network meta-analyses rather than a single pivotal trial, and some meta-analyses (e.g., 37678577) note residual uncertainty in effect size.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A retrospective controlled cohort (PMID:29772973) found metronomic cyclophosphamide maintenance after amputation/carboplatin gave no improvement in progression-free or overall survival in dogs with osteosarcoma. A companion toxicity-focused study (PMID:24803081) only assessed tolerability of cyclophosphamide-containing metronomic protocols, providing no additional efficacy signal.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple randomized trials incorporating cyclophosphamide (e.g., EOI two- vs multi-drug trial PMID 9314869, Latin American metronomic cyclophosphamide/methotrexate trial PMID 28263383) showed no survival or EFS benefit from cyclophosphamide-containing regimens versus comparators. Conversely, a network meta-analysis (PMID 28356114) found the cyclophosphamide-containing T12 regimen ranked highest for progression-free survival, indicating a positive signal at the same evidence tier.
judgement.caveats: No US label lists osteosarcoma as an indication for cyclophosphamide, so approval-level evidence is absent; cyclophosphamide is almost always used as part of multi-agent regimens in both species, making isolation of its individual contribution difficult, and veterinary evidence is limited to retrospective, non-randomized cohorts.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A single-arm uncontrolled study in 11 dogs with OA (PMID:24866508) found anti-NGF mAb significantly decreased CBPI pain severity and interference scores at 2 and 4 weeks versus baseline, meeting the criterion for a single-arm non-cancer study improving a validated outcome.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple phase 3 RCTs of tanezumab and fasinumab (e.g., PMID 22784777, 32234715, 33538113, 40001000, 41545313) and a phase 3 meta-analysis (PMID 33159281) consistently showed statistically significant improvements in WOMAC pain and physical function versus placebo/NSAID. No US approval exists for this indication, so phase 3 evidence is the highest level.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single small uncontrolled 11-dog study without a placebo control arm proper (crossover with PBS), while human evidence includes large-scale placebo-controlled phase 3 trials; joint safety concerns (RPOA) led to FDA non-approval of tanezumab in humans despite efficacy.

L0.indications: INDICATIONS AND USAGE Diazepam tablets are indicated for the management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety or tension associated with the stress of everyday life usually does not require treatment with an anxiolytic. In acute alcohol withdrawal, diazepam tablets may be useful in the symptomatic relief of acute agitation, tremor, impending or acute delirium tremens and hallucinosis. Diazepam tablets are a useful adjunct for the relief of skeletal muscle spasm due to reflex spasm to local pathology (such as inflammation of the muscles or joints, or secondary to trauma), spasticity caused by upper motor neuron disorders (such as cerebral palsy and paraplegia), athetosis, and stiff-man syndrome. Oral diazepam tablets may be used adjunctively in convulsive disorders, although it has not proved useful as the sole therapy. The effectiveness of diazepam tablets in long-term use, that is, more than 4 months, has not been assessed by systematic clinical studies. The physician should periodically reassess the usefulness of the drug for the individual patient.

judgement.human_basis: RCTs directly repleting magnesium in hypomagnesemic patients show positive results (e.g., corrected calcemia in intestinal hypomagnesemia PMID 1663053; improved respiratory muscle power PMID 6703506; improved metabolic syndrome components PMID 29793665) while others show no benefit (failed to improve insulin secretion in hypomagnesemic transplant patients PMID 28848225; no benefit in alcohol withdrawal syndrome PMID 37012631; no reduction in preeclampsia PMID 32272914). No US label specifically approves magnesium for treating hypomagnesemia as a disease.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is purely observational/diagnostic with no controlled efficacy trial of magnesium supplementation in dogs, precluding a definitive veterinary classification; human evidence spans many different downstream conditions (migraine, ADHD, blood pressure, T2DM, AWS, preeclampsia) rather than a single unified 'hypomagnesemia' disease trial, adding heterogeneity to the mixed classification.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized controlled pilot trial (PMID:25546713) in 16 cats with DKA showed the glargine+regular insulin (SC/IM) protocol significantly shortened time to resolution of hyperglycemia, ketonemia, pH/bicarbonate normalization, and hospitalization versus CRI regular insulin (all p<0.05).
judgement.human_basis: Multiple RCTs and a meta-analysis (41208563) of adding early subcutaneous glargine to IV insulin infusion for DKA show faster resolution and reduced insulin needs (36479786, 40840711, 41208563), but a pediatric double-blind RCT (40623843) failed its primary endpoint (time to DKA resolution, p=0.84) despite secondary benefits. US labels explicitly state glargine is not recommended for treating DKA (L0-L5).
judgement.caveats: The feline study, though randomized and controlled, is small (n=16) and labeled a pilot; human evidence is drawn from adjunctive-use trials in DKA (glargine plus IV insulin) rather than glargine monotherapy, and US labeling explicitly excludes DKA as an approved indication despite positive adjunctive trial data.

judgement.human_basis: No US label covers IVDD; at the highest evidence tier (randomized controlled trials), two RCTs show methylprednisolone (epidural) improves outcomes (PMID 18758356, 27555486), while another RCT found no significant difference from gabapentin on the primary pain endpoint (PMID 25883095), yielding mixed results.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single systemic IV MPSS RCT in acute severe IVDH, whereas human RCTs largely test epidural/local steroid administration for chronic or post-surgical disc disease, so route, dosing, and disease stage differ substantially between species.

However, a similarly designed RCT (PMID:35288019) found perineural dexmedetomidine did not reduce overall postoperative methadone requirements versus saline (failed primary endpoint), and another RCT (PMID:26529670) found no difference between two active analgesic techniques (indeterminate).
judgement.human_basis: No human clinical studies or trials of dexmedetomidine for ACL rupture pain/analgesia were retrieved; US labels only cover ICU/procedural sedation, not orthopedic surgical pain management for ACL repair.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is drawn from perioperative analgesia trials for cranial cruciate ligament surgery (nerve blocks/CRI), not disease-modifying treatment; no human evidence exists for the analogous ACL condition, precluding a meaningful comparison despite dexmedetomidine's approved human sedation indications for unrelated uses.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A single-arm prospective study in 6 dogs with naturally occurring DKA treated with IV insulin aspart CRI showed resolution of hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and acidemia in all dogs (median 28h) with no adverse effects (PMID:26379102).
judgement.human_basis: US labels for insulin aspart explicitly state it is NOT recommended for DKA (L1,L2,L5), so approval does not cover this indication; the highest applicable evidence is a randomized controlled trial (PMID 15277410) showing SC insulin aspart every 1-2h was as safe and effective as IV regular insulin for resolving hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis in 45 patients with uncomplicated DKA.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple RCTs show telmisartan reduces proteinuria and urinary injury markers versus enalapril/amlodipine or with add-on therapy (e.g., PMID 18855269, 20584070, 18712038, 16310573, 18423812), but the large ADPKD outcomes RCT (PMID 25399731) found no benefit on the composite of death/ESRD/50% GFR decline, and post-hoc TRANSCEND analysis (PMID 27927602) found no renal outcome benefit from telmisartan versus placebo. No US label covers CKD as a disease-modifying indication; only hypertension is approved (L1-L5).
judgement.caveats: Vet trial used a surrogate endpoint (proteinuria) and an active comparator rather than placebo, limiting direct comparability; human evidence is heterogeneous, ranging from small surrogate-outcome RCTs (positive) to a large hard-outcome RCT in ADPKD (negative), and no human CKD indication has regulatory approval.

judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence uses a specific ester (hydrocortisone aceponate) formulation as maintenance therapy, while human approval is for systemic IV/IM hydrocortisone succinate in severe allergic flares; multiple human RCTs comparing hydrocortisone to other agents show mixed comparative results but do not negate the top-level approval evidence.

judgement.veterinary_basis: In dogs (PMID:26648590), oral cobalamin normalized serum cobalamin in all 51 dogs with chronic enteropathy, meeting the positive threshold for a single-arm non-cancer efficacy study. In cats (PMID:28895200), parenteral cobalamin transiently raised levels but did not achieve full, sustained normalization of cellular cobalamin deficiency, an indeterminate result.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple randomized controlled trials (e.g., PMID 9694707, 14749150, 14616423, 16155269, 21232119, 26678525, 17158426) consistently show that oral or parenteral cobalamin supplementation effectively corrects biochemical cobalamin deficiency (raising serum B12, lowering MMA/homocysteine) and, in several trials, improves clinical/functional outcomes. No relevant US label exists for this specific indication, so phase 3 RCT evidence is the highest level.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is uncontrolled and species-specific with divergent results (dog positive, cat indeterminate); human RCTs primarily address correction of biochemical cobalamin deficiency broadly, not disease-modifying effects specifically in chronic enteropathy, limiting direct comparability.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The only veterinary record compares two cosyntropin doses for ACTH stimulation testing (a diagnostic procedure) in dogs suspected of or being treated for hyperadrenocorticism; it is a dose-finding/diagnostic-equivalence study, not a treatment efficacy trial for HAC.
judgement.human_basis: All US labels (L0-L5) indicate cosyntropin only as a diagnostic agent for screening adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison's disease), not as a treatment for Cushing's syndrome; the single retrieved human study also uses cosyntropin merely as a diagnostic test within an unrelated IBD-enema trial, providing no disease-modifying efficacy data for Cushing's syndrome.
judgement.caveats: Cosyntropin is a diagnostic ACTH-stimulation agent in both species, used to detect adrenal insufficiency/HAC rather than to treat Cushing's syndrome, so neither record set actually assesses disease-modifying efficacy for the stated human condition.

judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence comes from a single small RCT with a non-significant weight trend, while human evidence is drawn from larger, better-powered RCTs and meta-analyses showing consistent significant weight loss; species and dosing differences may also limit direct comparability.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized controlled trial in dogs found propofol-based TIVA required fewer anesthetic interventions to treat cardiovascular depression/arousal and maintained higher MAP than isoflurane, meeting its primary endpoint favoring propofol (PMID:27334295).
judgement.human_basis: Propofol injectable emulsion (Diprivan and generics) is FDA-approved for induction/maintenance of general anesthesia and sedation, which is the standard-of-care use to manage the perioperative period; label approval is the highest evidence tier available.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single small RCT (n=20) comparing propofol to isoflurane rather than placebo, so 'positive' reflects superiority to an active comparator on a surrogate intervention count, not a disease-outcome endpoint. Human evidence at the RCT level is mixed/indeterminate for many specific perioperative-complication endpoints (e.g., hypotension, cognition, gastric emptying show no difference or mixed results versus other agents), but the top-evidence tier used per rules is the US approval for general anesthesia/sedation, which is unambiguously positive.

judgement.veterinary_basis: In a randomized trial, oral rifaximin achieved complete/partial remission in 100% of dogs (85.7% complete) with chronic enteropathy, non-inferior to metronidazole (80% complete) with no significant difference between groups (PMID:27716258).
judgement.human_basis: A meta-analysis of RCTs found rifamycin derivatives (including rifaximin) significantly induced remission in active Crohn's disease, and a separate Cochrane meta-analysis found antibiotics as a class (including rifaximin trials) significantly reduced failure to achieve remission (RR 0.86, high certainty) (PMID:21407187, PMID:30731030). No US approval exists for IBD specifically, so meta-analysis level evidence is highest.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is from a single non-placebo-controlled active-comparator trial; human meta-analyses pool multiple antibiotics with rifaximin as one component, and a separate single-arm trial in a related condition (PSC, often comorbid with IBD) showed no efficacy, though this is not classified as IBD disease-modifying evidence per the top-level hierarchy.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The single RCT (PMID:27918639) compared two multi-drug protocols (inpatient with cefoxitin+maropitant vs outpatient with cefovecin+maropitant) rather than testing cefoxitin against placebo/no-treatment, and found no significant difference in the primary outcome (90% vs 80% survival, P=0.66). This design cannot isolate cefoxitin's efficacy and does not meet criteria for positive or negative classification.
judgement.human_basis: No human records were provided for parvoviral enteritis, and the US labels for cefoxitin cover only bacterial infections (respiratory, urinary, intra-abdominal, gynecological), not viral parvoviral enteritis.
judgement.caveats: Cefoxitin is an antibacterial agent with no direct antiviral activity against parvovirus; its veterinary use is for secondary bacterial infection prophylaxis/treatment in parvoviral enteritis, not disease-modifying antiviral therapy, and no human parvoviral enteritis data exist for this drug.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A retrospective study of 25 cats with hypocobalaminaemia and GI disease showed oral cyanocobalamin normalized (in fact supra-normalized) serum cobalamin in all 25 cats (median 128→2701 pmol/L, P<0.0001), meeting the bar for a single-arm study improving a validated outcome.
judgement.human_basis: US labels (L0, L2, L4) approve cyanocobalamin for vitamin B12 deficiency due to malabsorption associated with gastrointestinal pathology, dysfunction, or surgery, directly matching the human condition.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single uncontrolled retrospective study using biochemical normalization rather than a controlled clinical endpoint; human approval is broad and based on decades of malabsorption data rather than a dedicated pivotal RCT for this exact subgroup.

judgement.human_basis: US labels for buprenorphine (L0-L5) all pertain to opioid use disorder/dependence treatment, not to pain management for anterior cruciate ligament rupture; no human evidence for the analgesic indication in this condition is available.
judgement.caveats: No human clinical evidence specific to ACL rupture pain management with buprenorphine was retrieved; only unrelated US labels for opioid dependence exist, so the human side cannot be classified for the analgesic indication despite an approval existing at the top evidence tier.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Three RCTs of betamethasone-containing otic products in dogs with otitis externa; two showed equivalence to active comparators (PMID28295766, PMID30305092), and one showed clear superiority over placebo (62.9% vs 20.0% success, p<0.0001, PMID42638346).
judgement.human_basis: No US label specifically covers otitis externa (labels are for dermatoses/tinea), so highest evidence is RCT-level: betamethasone-based drops produced symptomatic improvement in all three RCTs (PMID18560873, PMID18324410, PMID224125), though comparator arms sometimes performed similarly or better.
judgement.caveats: Human trials mostly compare betamethasone-containing regimens to other active treatments rather than placebo, so 'positive' reflects consistent symptomatic benefit rather than superiority over no treatment; no US label explicitly lists otitis externa as an indication.

L5.indications: INDICATIONS AND USAGE Metronidazole vaginal gel is indicated in the treatment of bacterial vaginosis (formerly referred to as Haemophilus vaginitis, Gardnerella vaginitis, nonspecific vaginitis, Corynebacterium vaginitis, or anaerobic vaginosis). NOTE: For purposes of this indication, a clinical diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis is usually defined by the presence of a homogeneous vaginal discharge that (a) has a pH of greater than 4.5, (b) emits a “fishy” amine odor when mixed with a 10% KOH solution, and (c) contains clue cells on microscopic examination. Gram’s stain results consistent with a diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis include (a) markedly reduced or absent Lactobacillus morphology, (b) predominance of Gardnerella morphotype, and (c) absent or few white blood cells. Other pathogens commonly associated with vulvovaginitis, e.g., Trichomonas vaginalis, Chlamydia trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, Candida albicans, and Herpes simplex virus should be ruled out.

judgement.veterinary_basis: In a 2016 RCT (PMID:27716258), dogs treated with oral metronidazole 15 mg/kg q12h for 21 days achieved complete remission in 8/10 (80%) with significant reductions in CIBDAI and CRP (P=0.002), meeting the improved-validated-outcome criterion; no placebo arm was used, but metronidazole was non-inferior to rifaximin.
judgement.human_basis: A placebo-controlled RCT in acute severe ulcerative colitis (PMID:33245002) found IV ceftriaxone+metronidazole did not improve day-3 response versus placebo (28% vs 24%, p=1.00), while a broader meta-analysis of antibiotic RCTs in Crohn's disease (PMID:21407187) found antibiotics (including metronidazole-containing regimens) significantly superior to placebo for inducing remission (RR 0.85, P=0.03).
judgement.caveats: No US label covers IBD for metronidazole; human evidence is heterogeneous across trial designs (placebo-controlled vs active-comparator) and disease subtypes (UC vs CD), and epidemiologic meta-analyses even suggest metronidazole exposure increases IBD risk (PMID:25223575, PMID:38423349), complicating direct comparison with the single small veterinary RCT.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A single-arm study of intradiscal celecoxib-hydrogel in 10 client-owned dogs with IVD disease showed clinical improvement (reduced back pain) in 9 of 10 dogs by clinical exam and owner questionnaires, meeting the bar for a positive single-arm non-cancer outcome.
judgement.human_basis: The only human RCT used oral celecoxib plus methylcobalamin as background/control therapy compared against an herbal formula, so it does not isolate or test celecoxib's disease-modifying efficacy for IVD herniation; no US label indication exists for IVD disease.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a small uncontrolled pilot (n=10) using a local hydrogel delivery system, differing from systemic oral dosing in the human study; the human RCT was not designed to test celecoxib's efficacy per se, confounding attribution of any effect to celecoxib.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Only a retrospective/prospective observational case series (65 cats) with no controlled comparison; cats were reported to have a 'generally favourable response' to combined surgery plus clarithromycin/rifampicin but no quantifiable cure or response rate was given, so it cannot be classified as positive or negative under the rubric.
judgement.human_basis: No US-approved leprosy indication and no phase-3 trial specific to leprosy (the only phase-3 RCT, PMID 32171422, is for Buruli ulcer, a different disease); among earlier-phase/uncontrolled leprosy studies, several RCTs and pilot trials show clarithromycin to be bactericidal and clinically effective (PMID 8257487, 17402345, 8878595, 8203847, 29900892), while a dedicated RCT adding clarithromycin to standard ROM therapy found no significant additional benefit (PMID 21644471), yielding mixed evidence.
judgement.caveats: The only phase-3 clarithromycin trial identified (PMID 32171422) concerns Buruli ulcer (M. ulcerans), not leprosy, and was excluded from the leprosy-specific human evidence tier. Feline data are limited to descriptive case-series observations without a defined outcome metric, precluding a definitive positive/negative call.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple randomized controlled trials, including the large BIP trial (n=3090), consistently demonstrate significant reductions in triglycerides and cholesterol with bezafibrate versus placebo or comparators. judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is uncontrolled and short-term (30 days), limiting causal inference; human evidence is robust for lipid-lowering but the BIP trial's primary cardiovascular endpoint (not the lipid endpoint) was not significant, though this is a secondary outcome beyond the hyperlipidemia disease-modifying intent being assessed here.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Two randomized controlled trials in dogs (PMID:28543780, PMID:31580527) showed intranasal midazolam terminated status epilepticus in 70-76% of cases, significantly superior to rectal diazepam and at least as effective as IV midazolam.
judgement.human_basis: The phase-3 RAMPART trial (PMID 21967361, discussed further in PMID 24001080) demonstrated IM midazolam was noninferior/superior to IV lorazepam for prehospital status epilepticus, and a network meta-analysis (PMID 26511448) confirmed midazolam's efficacy across routes for seizure cessation. No phase-3 or meta-analysis evidence was negative.
judgement.caveats: US labels for midazolam cover sedation/anesthesia indications only and do not explicitly list status epilepticus, so approval-level evidence was not used; human evidence is drawn from phase-3 RCTs and a meta-analysis, many in pediatric populations, with some studies showing equivalence rather than superiority to comparators.

judgement.human_basis: Both human RCTs (25448495, 24943856) found gabapentin significantly reduced surgical stress markers (cortisol, catecholamines) and pain/analgesic consumption compared to placebo, with no phase-3 pivotal trials identified for a stress indication.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is inconsistent across three small crossover/parallel trials with differing endpoints (behavioral vs physiologic), and human evidence derives from small perioperative stress studies rather than dedicated 'stress' trials or an approved indication, limiting direct comparability.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Two RCTs (28629456, 33236379) assessed coagulation/electrolyte effects of mannitol vs HTS and did not test efficacy, but an observational study (41313647) showed mannitol significantly decreased optic nerve sheath diameter (a validated ICP biomarker) and improved neurological deficit scores in dogs with suspected ICH.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple US drug labels (L0, L1, L3, L4, L5) list mannitol injection as indicated for reduction of intracranial pressure and treatment of cerebral edema, representing the highest level of evidence (approval).
judgement.caveats: Veterinary RCTs directly comparing mannitol to HTS focused on safety/physiologic parameters (coagulation, electrolytes) rather than ICP efficacy endpoints, so the positive veterinary classification rests on a single small observational study using a surrogate imaging biomarker (ONSD) rather than a controlled efficacy trial; human evidence, while including US approval, also contains many RCTs/meta-analyses suggesting hypertonic saline may be superior to mannitol, though mannitol itself remains an approved and effective agent for ICP reduction.

L0.indications: INDICATIONS AND USAGE Diazepam tablets are indicated for the management of anxiety disorders or for the short-term relief of the symptoms of anxiety. Anxiety or tension associated with the stress of everyday life usually does not require treatment with an anxiolytic. In acute alcohol withdrawal, diazepam tablets may be useful in the symptomatic relief of acute agitation, tremor, impending or acute delirium tremens and hallucinosis. Diazepam tablets are a useful adjunct for the relief of skeletal muscle spasm due to reflex spasm to local pathology (such as inflammation of the muscles or joints, or secondary to trauma), spasticity caused by upper motor neuron disorders (such as cerebral palsy and paraplegia), athetosis, and stiff-man syndrome. Oral diazepam tablets may be used adjunctively in convulsive disorders, although it has not proved useful as the sole therapy. The effectiveness of diazepam tablets in long-term use, that is, more than 4 months, has not been assessed by systematic clinical studies. The physician should periodically reassess the usefulness of the drug for the individual patient.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The only RCT involving diazepam (28543780) compared rectal diazepam against intranasal midazolam, not placebo/no-treatment, and diazepam was the losing comparator (20% vs 70% success), which does not meet the criteria for negative. A second non-randomized CRI duration study (37675074) found no significant outcome differences, providing no clear efficacy signal.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple US drug labels (L2, L3, L5) explicitly list diazepam injection as 'a useful adjunct in status epilepticus,' constituting an approved indication for this condition.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence for diazepam specifically (as opposed to comparator midazolam) in canine status epilepticus is limited to active-comparator or non-randomized dose-duration studies, none of which test diazepam against placebo/no-treatment, precluding a positive or negative classification; human evidence rests on FDA label approval rather than a dedicated pivotal RCT for diazepam alone in status epilepticus.

judgement.human_basis: A phase-3, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (PMID 8204472) confirmed cyclosporine's efficacy over placebo in severe atopic dermatitis, and a phase-3 noninferiority trial (PMID 28967549) showed cyclosporine superior to methotrexate at week 8, though some meta-analyses (e.g., PMID 33074565, 37678577) note evidence certainty is limited.
judgement.caveats: Cyclosporine lacks a specific US label indication for atopic dermatitis (labels cover psoriasis, RA, transplant, and ophthalmic uses only), so classification relies on RCT-level evidence; feline data are limited to a small uncontrolled pilot study.

judgement.human_basis: The pivotal multinational phase IIb/III CASSIOPEIR trial failed its primary renal composite endpoint overall (PMID 31119846), but the pre-specified Japanese subgroup of the same trial showed a significant benefit with the 240 μg dose (PMID 33340238). A prior phase II dose-finding trial also failed its primary endpoint (PMID 26475266), while smaller phase 3-level evidence is mixed, and a Cochrane meta-analysis found insufficient data to draw conclusions (PMID 35224730).
judgement.caveats: Veterinary support relies on one positive feline RCT and one uncontrolled/non-randomized canine survival study; human evidence at the highest (phase 3) tier is internally discordant, with the overall pivotal trial negative but a subgroup analysis positive, precluding a clean concordance judgment.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A dose-escalation study in 27 dogs with multicentric lymphoma reported an 83.3% overall response rate (3 PR + 2 CR) at the MTD (PMID:28505195). A randomized double-blind trial showed etoposide phosphate achieving response rates and PFS comparable to an active comparator (PMID:32133044), consistent with efficacy.
judgement.human_basis: The highest-level human evidence consists of two phase 3 trials (PMID 33512419, PMID 36541957) that compare etoposide-containing backbone regimens against variant regimens (allo- vs auto-SCT; ibrutinib addition) rather than testing etoposide itself against placebo or no treatment, so neither can be classified as positive or negative for etoposide's efficacy. No US approval exists for lymphoma specifically (labels cover only testicular tumors and SCLC), leaving phase 3 as the top tier with no classifiable signal.
judgement.caveats: Human phase 3 trials use etoposide as an established backbone within combination regimens rather than testing etoposide's own efficacy, making direct comparison to the canine efficacy data difficult; lower-level phase 2 single-arm studies (e.g., ORR 69-97%) suggest efficacy but are not the highest evidence tier per the rules.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 23 dogs (16 cholecalciferol) showed significant reduction in pruritus and lesion (CADESI) scores versus placebo (PMID:29419484).
judgement.human_basis: Several double-blind RCTs of oral cholecalciferol in AD show significant improvement in SCORAD/EASI (PMID 25282565, 22395583, 32530339, 35763390-partial), while others show no benefit over placebo (PMID 38483248, 23638978, 31124381). No US label covers AD; evidence is mixed at the RCT level.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence rests on a single small crossover RCT (n=23, cross-over design) while human evidence comprises multiple larger RCTs with inconsistent outcomes depending on population (children vs adults, baseline vitamin D status, dose, duration); no product is approved for AD, so human classification uses RCT-level evidence only.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A single-arm phase II trial in 13 dogs with B-cell lymphoma showed no complete or partial responses (0% ORR) and only one dog with stable disease, so it falls below the response threshold; per rules, an uncontrolled study below threshold is indeterminate, not negative.
judgement.human_basis: Two pilot/observational studies in C. psittaci-associated ocular adnexal B-cell lymphoma showed objective responses (2/9 CR, 2/9 PR in one study) and long-term efficacy (60.9% 5-year PFS) with first-line doxycycline, representing the highest available evidence level (uncontrolled/observational, no phase-2/3 or approval).
judgement.caveats: Human evidence is limited to a specific marginal-zone B-cell lymphoma subtype linked to C. psittaci infection, which may not generalize to broader B-cell lymphoma; veterinary study used a different, more aggressive multicentric lymphoma population and short treatment duration, limiting direct comparability.

judgement.human_basis: Furosemide is FDA-approved for treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure in adults and pediatric patients (L0-L5), representing the highest level of human evidence (approval).
judgement.caveats: Vet evidence for furosemide itself is largely indirect (active-comparator arm in a non-inferiority trial against torsemide, plus an uncontrolled retrospective study) rather than a placebo-controlled efficacy trial; human approval is for symptomatic edema relief rather than disease-modifying outcomes, and most human RCTs address diuretic administration strategy rather than furosemide vs placebo efficacy.

judgement.veterinary_basis: In cats (SEISICAT, PMID29277469) spironolactone met its primary mortality endpoint versus placebo (22% vs 82% deaths, p=0.0216), a positive RCT. In Dobermans with DCM (PMID34315691) the RCT failed its primary survival endpoint (183 vs 124 days, p=0.254), a negative RCT.
judgement.human_basis: Spironolactone is FDA-approved for NYHA III-IV heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (L0-L5), based on the pivotal RALES trial showing a 30% mortality reduction (p<0.001, PMID10471456). This phase-3 evidence underlies the approved systolic heart-failure indication, though a separate HFpEF trial (TOPCAT) was negative for a different, non-approved indication.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is species- and disease-stage-specific (cats vs Dobermans with DCM) and both trials are small; human approval is restricted to reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, while TOPCAT showed no benefit in preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure, a phenotype more analogous to feline cardiomyopathy.

judgement.human_basis: Multiple hydrocodone/acetaminophen products (L1-L5) carry a US label indication for management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic, covering postoperative pain, and phase 3 RCTs (e.g., PMID:25526227, PMID:10972635) confirm efficacy over placebo for pain relief.
judgement.caveats: The veterinary evidence is limited to a single head-to-head (non-placebo) trial showing inferiority to an active comparator, which cannot be classified as negative under the strict placebo/no-treatment rule, while the human evidence is robust and positive at the highest evidence tier (US approval), making the overall pair indeterminate rather than clearly discordant.

judgement.veterinary_basis: A randomized, blinded trial (PMID 30082181) in 29 dogs found hydromorphone CRI provided pain relief equivalent to fentanyl CRI for postsurgical/medical pain, with low pain scores and no significant differences in efficacy or adverse effects.
judgement.human_basis: Hydromorphone hydrochloride products (L0-L5) are FDA-approved for management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic, which encompasses postoperative pain; multiple RCTs (e.g., PMID 39433860, 27454263) also demonstrate analgesic efficacy in postoperative settings.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single active-comparator (non-placebo) RCT showing equivalence to fentanyl rather than superiority to placebo, so efficacy is inferred rather than directly proven against no-treatment; human approval is broad and not postoperative-pain-specific, but numerous postoperative RCTs support efficacy for this indication.

judgement.veterinary_basis: PMID 29553899 is an observational (non-controlled) study showing IOP was unchanged after propofol in nonpremedicated glaucomatous dogs, not a treatment efficacy trial for glaucoma. PMID 36950543 is an RCT comparing propofol vs tiletamine-zolazepam on peri-induction IOP in healthy (non-glaucomatous) dogs, so neither study establishes propofol as an effective glaucoma therapy.
judgement.human_basis: Numerous RCTs measure propofol's effect on IOP during anesthesia for unrelated surgeries in non-glaucomatous patients, with inconsistent results—some show significant IOP reduction versus comparators (e.g., PMID 12059895, 23579523, 31045821) while others show no significant difference or no decrease at all (e.g., PMID 26561424, 2331082, 22274735). None of these trials test propofol as a therapeutic intervention for diagnosed glaucoma, precluding a definitive efficacy classification for the glaucoma indication.
judgement.caveats: Propofol is used as a general anesthetic, and both veterinary and human records study its effect on intraocular pressure as an anesthesia-related physiologic parameter rather than as a treatment for glaucoma itself; only one veterinary study involved dogs with actual glaucoma and it was purely observational, while all human studies were conducted in non-glaucomatous surgical populations.

judgement.human_basis: Three randomized controlled trials of sacubitril/valsartan in functional/secondary mitral regurgitation (PMID 30586756, 38635062, 42104906) each met their primary efficacy endpoints, showing reduced regurgitant orifice area/volume, lower NT-proBNP, and improved exercise hemodynamics versus comparator/standard care.
judgement.caveats: Human evidence pertains to secondary/functional mitral regurgitation from heart failure rather than primary degenerative mitral valve prolapse, which differs mechanistically from the canine myxomatous mitral valve disease model; no human trials specifically address primary MVP with sacubitril/valsartan, and no US label covers mitral regurgitation or prolapse.

judgement.veterinary_basis: Only evidence is a small (n=13) pilot RCT of sacubitril/valsartan focusing on RAAS/aldosterone biomarkers, with no significant difference in NT-proBNP or echocardiographic outcomes between groups. This is a dose-finding/pharmacodynamic pilot study, not a trial demonstrating a validated clinical efficacy endpoint.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple randomized controlled trials of sacubitril/valsartan in functional/secondary mitral regurgitation (PMID 30586756, 38635062, 42104906) consistently showed superiority over comparator in reducing regurgitant severity and improving hemodynamic/clinical parameters. No US label exists specifically for mitral valve disease, so phase-3 RCT evidence is the highest level, and it is uniformly positive.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is a single small pilot study with biomarker (not clinical) primary endpoint, precluding positive/negative classification. Human evidence pertains mainly to functional/secondary mitral regurgitation in heart failure patients rather than primary degenerative mitral valve prolapse, limiting direct comparability to the canine MMVD model.

judgement.caveats: Vincristine is almost always used in combination regimens in both species, making attribution to vincristine alone difficult; some phase 3 trials show newer agents (PLD, gemcitabine) outperform vincristine-based regimens, but vincristine combinations themselves still meet efficacy thresholds.

L0.indications: INDICATIONS Initial Treatment of Advanced Ovarian Carcinoma Carboplatin injection is indicated for the initial treatment of advanced ovarian carcinoma in established combination with other approved chemotherapeutic agents. One established combination regimen consists of carboplatin and cyclophosphamide. Two randomized controlled studies conducted by the NCIC and SWOG with carboplatin versus cisplatin, both in combination with cyclophosphamide, have demonstrated equivalent overall survival between the two groups (see CLINICAL STUDIES ). There is limited statistical power to demonstrate equivalence in overall pathologic complete response rates and long-term survival (≥ 3 years) because of the small number of patients with these outcomes: the small number of patients with residual tumor < 2 cm after initial surgery also limits the statistical power to demonstrate equivalence in this subgroup. Secondary Treatment of Advanced Ovarian Carcinoma Carboplatin injection is indicated for the palliative treatment of patients with ovarian carcinoma recurrent after prior chemotherapy, including patients who have been previously treated with cisplatin. Within the group of patients previously treated with cisplatin, those who have developed progressive disease while receiving cisplatin therapy may have a decreased response rate.

judgement.veterinary_basis: The only feline injection-site sarcoma record is an ex vivo colony-forming assay correlating γH2AX expression with carboplatin resistance in cultured tumor cells; it is not an in vivo clinical trial and reports no clinical response rate, so it cannot be classified as positive or negative.
judgement.human_basis: US labels cover only ovarian carcinoma, not soft tissue sarcoma, so the highest applicable evidence level is phase 3 RCTs; multiple phase 3 trials adding carboplatin to sarcoma regimens (CWS/RMS-96 CEVAIE vs VAIA, MMT95 six-drug vs three-drug, HD chemotherapy with carboplatin/etoposide (MICE) vs standard dose) all failed to show improved event-free or overall survival.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is limited to a single mechanistic ex vivo study with no clinical outcome data, precluding a definitive efficacy call; human phase 3 evidence pertains to carboplatin added to multi-agent pediatric sarcoma regimens rather than single-agent carboplatin, while phase 2 single-arm carboplatin monotherapy trials in adults show ORRs of 12-38%, illustrating discordance across human evidence levels that is resolved by prioritizing the phase 3 data per the rubric.

Another RCT (PMID 30197106) found midazolam-medetomidine combinations in dogs were inferior to butorphanol-medetomidine, with the lower dose showing 85% sedation failure.
judgement.human_basis: Multiple US labels (L0-L5) approve midazolam injection for preoperative sedation/anxiolysis and procedural sedation, representing the highest level of evidence. This approval reflects established efficacy for symptomatic sedation across diagnostic, therapeutic, and perioperative settings.
judgement.caveats: Veterinary evidence is mixed with dose- and species-dependent outcomes, while human approval is broad and unconditional; many human RCTs comparing midazolam to newer agents (dexmedetomidine, remimazolam) show mixed relative efficacy but do not negate the approved indication.

Severe hypofunction of the pituitary - adrenal axis is usually associated with subnormal plasma cortisol values but a low basal level is not per se evidence of adrenal insufficiency and does not suffice to make the diagnosis. judgement.veterinary_basis: The single dog study (PMID:30230611) only compared low-dose vs standard-dose cosyntropin for diagnostic ACTH-stimulation testing in dogs suspected of hypoadrenocorticism; it did not test cosyntropin as a disease-modifying treatment for the disease itself.
judgement.human_basis: Cosyntropin/tetracosactide is used almost exclusively as a diagnostic agent for adrenal insufficiency; the only disease-modifying attempt (PMID 24170102) was a small single-arm pilot in which only 2 of 13 patients with autoimmune Addison's disease achieved a durable cortisol response allowing steroid withdrawal, while most showed no improvement.
judgement.caveats: Nearly all human and veterinary evidence concerns cosyntropin's diagnostic use (ACTH stimulation testing) rather than disease-modifying treatment of Addison's disease/hypoadrenocorticism, limiting direct comparability for the stated disease-modifying intent; the one human regenerative-medicine pilot study was small, uncontrolled, and yielded mixed individual outcomes.
